title: Signal flags and a witch's reservoir

place.label: Site of the Spring Valley Water pumping station, 31–33 Leland Avenue

hook: Before the valley had pipes to spare, a man on Leland Avenue and a woman up the hill ran its water supply by waving flags at each other.
story: When the valley was first built up, its water came from a Spring Valley Water pumping station at 31–33 Leland Avenue, next door to the Bay Shore Hotel [1][2]. An early photograph of the hotel going up shows the pumphouse right beside it [3]. The reservoir that fed it sat at the top of the hill above Wilde Avenue, just off the road now called Mansell [1]. In the 1920s the station's supervisor was Dan Condon. A woman up at the reservoir helped control the flow. When he signalled with a flag, she opened the gates and water ran down to the station. Another signal meant the station was full [1]. Local historian Betty Parshall was one of the 'Wilde Avenue gang' who roamed that hill in the 1940s. She remembered the reservoir under a wooden roof, black with age and peaked like 'a huge old Gothic house that had sunk into the ground'. She and her friend Marian Rado peered through cracks at the dark water and half-believed a witch lived inside [1]. The reservoir was later drained and torn down, and an unloved concrete viewing tower rose on its pad [1]. Parshall's flag story now appears on one of the 'musing station' plaques along McLaren Park's Philosopher's Way [4].

title: The school that carved wildflowers, not soap

place.label: Visitacion Valley Elementary School and playground, Schwerin Street at Visitacion Avenue

hook: In the 1930s, children here pressed, painted and sketched nearly forty kinds of wildflowers. In art class they carved flowers where other schools carved soap animals.
story: A newspaper clipping from about 1936 or 1937, later donated to the Visitacion Valley History Project by Viola Rusca, describes an unusual school. Pupils at Visitacion Valley Elementary counted nearly 40 kinds of wildflowers in the hills and valley. The season ran from January until the last poppy faded in late summer and fall [1]. On trips into the San Bruno hills they picked only enough sprays for an exhibit, never pulling up roots. Then they pressed and mounted the flowers, wrote stories about them, painted them and sketched them where they grew. Other schools carved soap into animals or missions. These children carved wildflowers [1]. 'This intensive study and appreciation of wild flowers… instills a love of beauty in the children which is theirs for life,' said the principal, Miss Mary A. Nolan [1]. Not every child was so gentle. Harry Pierce and Clarence Wikse picked wildflowers to sell, and wild iris fetched the best price. Wikse later became a florist [1]. The botanist Alice Eastwood recalled in 1945 that the San Bruno Hills south of the valley were noted for 'great beds' of iris. 'Homes are replacing them now,' she warned [2]. A new school building facing Schwerin Street was finished by 1937. The old one came down, and its site is now the Visitacion Valley playground [1].

title: The Galloping Goose's last run

place.label: Schwerin Street, route of the Visitacion Valley streetcar line

hook: For nearly 28 years a single-track streetcar wobbled through the valley via Schwerin Street. Its nicknames were affectionate, and a little rude.
story: The valley's own streetcar line opened on October 25, 1909. It ran on a single track with passing turnouts, from the Six Mile House at today's Bayshore Boulevard and Sunnydale Avenue to Geneva Avenue and Mission Street [1][2]. The route ran up McDonald Avenue, turned left at Schwerin Street and and then right at Geneva, which was still called Walbridge Street at the time [1][2]. The Market Street Railway usually ran just two cars on what the Grapevine's historian called its 'haphazard track'. A third car was reportedly destroyed in an accident in 1918 [1]. Valley streetcars picked up nicknames such as the 'Galloping Goose' and the 'Molasses Special'; Appiano called this line the 'beloved galloping goose' [1][3]. Because of the long waits while cars were switched on the single track, the whole district got a nickname too: 'Hesitation Valley' [3]. By the late 1930s buses were taking over, and the line carried few passengers. The Market Street Railway handed the route to an extended 50 Crocker-Amazon bus. On July 31, 1937, after nearly 28 years, the streetcars made their last run [1][2]. Rails did return in the end. Muni's T-Third light rail now ends at Bayshore and Sunnydale, where the Goose's route used to begin [4].

title: Bufano's bear at the Sunnydale projects

place.label: Sunnydale community center, about 1654 Sunnydale Avenue

hook: Among the barracks-style blocks of Sunnydale stands a work by one of San Francisco's most famous sculptors: a growling bear above a woman's face.
story: Beniamino 'Benny' Bufano's rounded, whimsical animals turn up all over San Francisco. One of them is at the Sunnydale public housing development. It stands in front of the community center at 1654 Sunnydale Avenue [1]. The piece shows a bear above a human head. One writer calls it 'Bear over the Head of Peace' and dates it to about 1935–1940 [1]. A July 2009 Nob Hill Gazette survey, quoted in the Grapevine, called it 'Bear and Virgin'. It described 'the head of a growling black bear over a woman's head, symbolizing peace' [2]. That article counted three Bufano works in San Francisco public housing projects [2]. Bufano was born in Italy in 1886, one of sixteen children, and his family emigrated to New York when he was three. He came to San Francisco in 1915 to assist a sculptor working on the Panama-Pacific Exposition [2]. A legend claimed he had cut off a finger and mailed it to President Wilson to protest the First World War. His wife said he had lost two finger joints to an electric saw [2]. Either way, the legend fixed his reputation as a lifelong pacifist [2]. Oddly, that date is earlier than Sunnydale itself, which the same writer says was built in the 1940s to house military personnel and their families [1].

title: Eichler's brick townhouses, a little Pittsburgh

place.label: Geneva Terrace townhouses, Schwerin Street at Velasco Avenue

hook: California's best-known modernist builder came to the valley and built brick row houses with arched windows. One historian asked: 'Are we in Pittsburgh?'
story: Joseph Eichler is famous for glass-walled, flat-roofed homes in the suburbs. In Visitacion Valley he built something quite different. Geneva Terrace, built in 1965 and 1966 around Sunnydale and Velasco avenues and Schwerin Street, is a set of two-storey townhouses. They were designed by the architect Claude Oakland with Kinji Imada [1][2]. Brick fronts, rows of arched windows and open carports give them what Heritage's Woody LaBounty called 'an East Coast feel'. 'Are we in Pittsburgh? Albany? Poughkeepsie?' he asked [1]. Each owner has a private rear patio, and the development shares open community space [1]. The houses were part of a larger landscape plan, matched by apartment towers [1]. Those were Eichler's Geneva Towers, which were later imploded [3]. One visiting blogger counted eight streets of identical two-storey, four-bedroom homes. With the ornamental bars on doors and windows, the blogger thought they felt like the French Quarter of New Orleans [2]. LaBounty sees the whole group as a possible historic district. That is harder to win than a single landmark, he notes, because so many owners would have to agree [1].

title: 'Valley Vision' on the library wall

place.label: 'Valley Vision' mural, Desmond Street side of 37–45 Leland Avenue (former branch library)

hook: In 1987 the neighbourhood shut Desmond Street to celebrate a mural that it had helped design, sketch by sketch, in the library window.
story: The 1933 building at Leland Avenue and Desmond Street long housed the valley's branch library [1]. In the summer of 1987 muralist Jo Tucker began painting its Desmond Street wall. Two summer youth workers and an adult volunteer helped her [2][4]. Tucker was born in Barberton, Ohio, and worked as a community organiser in Boston. In San Francisco she joined a project protesting the air war in Vietnam; people there were painting a mural about the war, and that set her course [3]. 'Murals have to do with community,' she said. For the library wall she held meetings with staff and residents, then posted her sketches in the library window and changed them based on what people said. An airplane was added, and a cane went into one man's hand to raise awareness of disability. Community gardens were added when their land leases became an issue [3][4]. The finished 'Valley Vision' shows the valley's plants, animals, people, industries, shops and churches from the 1770s onward, up to the era when Geneva Towers dominated the skyline [4]. On November 7, 1987, Desmond Street was closed for a celebration planned by Anne Kaartunen, who had helped Tucker win grants [3][4]. By then Tucker had also led pupils in painting a mural of valley history in the Visitacion Valley Elementary schoolyard [2].

title: The whale house on Delta Street

place.label: The 'whale house', 150 Delta Street at Tioga Avenue

hook: A huge blue whale swims across a hillside house on Delta Street. Behind the kitchen sheetrock, its owner found a brick room nobody can explain.
story: Neighbours call 150 Delta Street, at Tioga Avenue, 'the whale house'. A mural dominated by a huge blue whale covers the side most visible from the street. The front and south walls are painted too [1]. The owner, the artist Opal Essence, wanted to honour an earlier resident: Dr. Blanche M. Baker, a psychiatrist who, in the 1950s, publicly challenged the belief that homosexuality was a mental illness [1][2]. Sources disagree on when Baker moved in and when Essence arrived [1][2]. Essence invited artist friends, and they painted over a weekend. Among them were Mars-1, Damon Soule, Amanda Sage and the graffiti artist Estria, who painted a 'universal goddess' on the south side [1]. Heritage dates the whale, which it calls Geistal, to 1991 [2]. Graffiti artists, Essence explained, 'work fast before they can be chased away' [1]. The house holds a second puzzle. When Essence pulled down her kitchen sheetrock, she found a room of aged brick with an arched opening, a fireplace and hand-hewn beams [2][3]. Records date the house to 1934, and a 1914 map shows an empty lot. A 1949 insurance map marks it as the only brick house for blocks. Nobody yet knows why [2].

title: Six water lots become a greenway

place.label: Hans Schiller Plaza, Visitacion Valley Greenway, Leland Avenue at Peabody Street

hook: Six empty blocks of Water Department land ran through the valley. Neighbours and artists spent years turning them into a chain of gardens, one gate at a time.
story: Six block-long parcels spill down the hillside through the heart of the valley. They are former Water Department land, left undeveloped [1][2]. In the 1990s neighbours organised the Visitacion Valley Greenway Project to turn them into parks. Getting permission to build on what was then a Public Utilities Commission easement took five years of negotiations [2][3]. The first site finished was Hans Schiller Plaza, at Leland and Peabody, which opened in March 2001 [3]. The Columbia Foundation paid for it in memory of Hans J. Schiller, a Bay Area architect and environmental activist whom Governor Jerry Brown had appointed to the Bay Conservation and Development Commission [3]. That May the new plaza held its first big event, 'Weaving Our Roots', a Native American celebration with Sámi and Diné (Navajo) dancing and drumming and jingle-dress dancing [4]. Artists shaped the whole greenway. Sculptor Fran Martin coordinated the project from 1994 and made its tile work and weir walls. Jim Growden, a sculptor in wood and steel, forged eight of its twelve signature gates [3]. A community garden followed in 2008, and the Greenway now serves as an outdoor classroom [1].

title: Parking meters sprouting like wheat

place.label: 'Street Life' sculpture, Leland Avenue at Bayshore Boulevard

hook: The gateway to 'downtown' Visitacion Valley is a grove of surplus city parking meters, painted orange and raised on tall, arching poles.
story: In 2009, as the city redesigned Leland Avenue's streetscape, it set aside money for public art [1]. A panel of neighbours and arts professionals picked a proposal by Matthew Passmore and his artist group Rebar. Their plan was twenty poles topped with recycled parking meters, donated by the Municipal Transportation Agency [1]. The community saw the design at the branch library in September 2009, and the Arts Commission approved it on November 2 [2]. Among the panel's requests: make the meters more orange-red, so they wouldn't look like giant matchsticks [1]. According to the Arts Commission, the meters were meant to look as if they had grown to 'a whimsically tall height', like swaying grain. That nods to the valley's farming past and to the nearby Greenway [1][2]. The work, called 'Street Life', was slated for the corner of Leland and Bayshore, in front of the Shun Lee Market, and was standing there by 2011 [2][3]. Its budget was $35,000 in the planning documents; one later account put it at $38,000 [1][3]. 'The street furnishings of today may well be the art supplies of tomorrow,' Passmore said [3].

title: Fifty horses on a gambler's street
hook: In 1902 a family built a house on weekends on a two-block road named, it was said, for a notorious Gold Rush gambler. Soon it held fifty horses.
story: In 1902 Joseph Edelmann and Dorothy's uncles built a house in the valley on weekends. Dorothy's grandmother, Katherine Bergold, had bought seven $50 parcels along what soon became Cora Street [1]. With the grandmother's house nearby, the property kept up to 50 horses and was known in the family as 'the farm'. 'We never had a Christmas or New Years with less than 50 people,' Dorothy, later Mrs. Frandsen, remembered [1]. She went to one of the valley's first elementary schools, a shack at the foot of Cora Street, sitting on a wooden bucket [1]. Grapevine columnist Len Appiano wrote that the two-block street was named 'for a controversial Gold Rush gambler' [1]. The city's best-known gambler named Cora was Charles Cora. In 1856 the Vigilance Committee hanged him before a crowd of about 20,000 [3]. Neighbouring streets honour early officials. Appiano wrote that Burr Avenue is named for Ephraim Burr, the mayor who presided when city and county were consolidated in the 1850s, and Garrison Avenue for Mayor Cornelius Garrison, a shipbuilder elected six months after he arrived [2]. Streets could change names too: Delta Street was once Cowden Street [4].

title: Where the wild poppies grew

place.label: Wilde Avenue at Rutland Street (former Visitacion View Grocery, later KC Market)

hook: A 1926 sales booklet promised paved streets and 'beautiful bungalows' on the valley's sunny hillside. The same year, a hilltop grocer opened at Wilde and Rutland.
story: In 1926 the Visitacion Reis Tract Improvement Association published a booklet selling the valley's northern slopes. 'Where the wild poppies grew are paved streets, fire hydrants, high tension wires, and beautiful bungalows,' it boasted. It praised the tract's 'sunny southern exposure' and pointed buyers to the builders' ads [1]. Wilde Avenue was the tract's main paved street, and the booklet sold its transit links. At the Five Mile House, where Wilde met San Bruno Avenue and Third Street, residents could choose from three Market Street Railway lines [1]. Stucco subdivisions went on filling the hillsides around older farmhouses into the 1950s [3]. That same year, 1926, a store was built at the corner of Wilde Avenue and Rutland Street: the Visitacion View Grocery and Meat Market, phone RAndolph 4855 [2]. It became a lesson in how not to run a corner shop. The owner, Pete, refused a boy some carrots until his family's two-week-old tab was paid. Another day he yelled across the intersection at Parshall's mother, who was carrying groceries bought 'down the Valley'. Neither family went back [2]. Pete kept his business until retirement anyway, and the store, later the KC Market, lasted until 2008 [2].

title: 'Pay after the war': the railroad shop boom

place.label: Bayshore Boulevard near Sunnydale Avenue, facing the former Southern Pacific Bayshore yard

hook: In 1917 a downtown realtor promised that $70 cash for a lot facing the new Southern Pacific shops would soon be worth thousands.
story: In 1907 the Southern Pacific laid its 'Bayshore cutoff' across bay fill at the valley's edge. Soon afterwards it built an enormous rail yard and shop complex that cut the first valley streets off from the bay [1]. The Grapevine's Matthew Brady put the complex at $2,300,000 and 260 acres. Heritage says it sprawled over more than 200 acres [1][2]. It became the main maintenance centre for the company's Coast Division and employed hundreds of workers, many of whom lived in the valley [1]. Speculators moved in early. In 1917 J. W. Wright & Co. of 228 Montgomery Street advertised: 'Where S.P. shops are building – secure a business location now. Pay after the war if you want to' [2]. The ad promised that 'thousands of high-priced skilled artisans' would work at the shops. A $700 lot facing them, it said, would soon be 'worth thousands', and '$70 cash secures today a car-line business location' [2]. For decades the yards hemmed in the valley [3]. Before the century closed, though, train maintenance and storage had moved elsewhere, and the Southern Pacific was gone from the valley [1].
